1015-the-oregon-trail-sketches-of-prairi:
In 1846 Francis Parkman, a young Boston man of frail health, rode west with the emigrant trains to see the prairie and the Rockies before they changed. He camped with traders and Sioux, chased buffalo, and lived rough for months, then wrote this account of what he saw.

The book sketches wagon camps, Indian lodges, hunts, and storms in vivid, firsthand prose. Parkman admires the skill of the Plains peoples even as he speaks with the bias of his age. It stands as a classic of American travel writing and a first draft of the West that would soon vanish.
10234-old-creole-days-a-story-of-creole-:
George W. Cable published this story collection in 1907, though its tales of old New Orleans date from earlier years. Cable writes of Creole life in the French Quarter, where old houses, balconies, and narrow streets hold a fading world. His tone mixes affection, irony, and moral care.

Madame Delphine, Cafe des Exiles, Belles Demoiselles Plantation, Posson Jone, and Jean-ah Poquelin stand among the best-known pieces. Love, caste, and family honor drive the plots. Readers get a classic, atmospheric portrait of Creole New Orleans, still praised for its local color and craft.
11141-a-summer-in-leslie-goldthwaite-s-l:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney wrote this 1866 story of a summer in Leslie Goldthwaite's life, first of a series of four on girl-life and home-life. Whitney dedicates the book to her friend Maria S. Cummins and days among the mountains made beautiful by her companionship. The series, first furnished for Our Young Folks magazine, edited by Ticknor and Lucy Larcom, later added We Girls, Real Folks, and The Other Girls.

Chapters follow the green of the leaf, wayside glimpses, eyestones, Marmaduke Wharne, hummocks, Dakie Thayne, down at Outledge, and sixteen and sixty. Leslie visits Aunt Hoskins, whose niece Prissy, deaf since scarlet fever, runs by like a squirrel and perches under the bird-cage. Whitney keeps home-life as the centre and goal of effort, guiding girl readers toward womanly work and character through a mountain summer.
11277-egyptian-ideas-of-the-future-life:
E. A. Wallis Budge, keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian antiquities at the British Museum, wrote this first volume of the Books on Egypt and Chaldea series on Egyptian religion. Chapters treat belief in God, Osiris as god of resurrection, the many gods of Egypt, the judgment of the dead, and resurrection and immortality. Illustrations show the judgment in the hall of Maati and the deceased led before Osiris.

Budge drew on temple texts and funerary literature to explain what Egyptians expected after death, from the soul's journey to the Elysian fields of Sekhet-Aaru. The book was meant for students beginning Egyptian studies, following his earlier language primers. It remains a clear early synthesis, written before many later discoveries revised its details.
11859-isaac-t-hopper-a-true-life:
Lydia Maria Child published this biography of Quaker philanthropist Isaac T. Hopper in 1853, drawing on conversations she noted down without his knowledge. Hopper spent his life helping others in New York and Philadelphia, and Child warns that his story cannot be told without the stories of the people he aided.

Much of the book follows Hopper's antislavery work: buying freedom for enslaved people, carrying cases into court, and blocking slaveholders with writs and legal delays. Short, vivid anecdotes of his humor and bluntness run between the cases. Letters from friends and family close a portrait of practical benevolence rather than abstract reform.
11882-colonel-quaritch-v-c-a-tale-of-cou:
H. Rider Haggard's Colonel Quaritch, V.C., first published in 1888, is a tale of country life centered on Harold Quaritch, a soldier who meditates on his position before meeting the local squire. Chapters follow the tale of Sir James de la Molle, the squire's explanation of his affairs, and the lawyer Quest, whose dealings shape the plot.

A young woman offers Edward Cossey anything in her power to save her father from seeing his estate, Honham, sold over his head, and Cossey laughs at the size of the order. Talk of hopeless affection, necessity, and self-denial runs through the later chapters, as Haggard sets a love story against mortgages, lawyers, and the quiet pressures of rural property.
1205-the-colour-of-life:
Alice Meynell was a Victorian essayist of fine taste. She opens this book by arguing that the true color of life is not red, the color of violence, but the grey-green of grass and quiet days. Her essays follow: on biography, on clouds, on the actress Eleonora Duse, and on the passing of time.

Meynell writes in short, polished prose, with a poet's eye for small things and a Catholic's sense of the sacred in the common. The essays are brief and reflective, never loud. The book gives a gentle, thoughtful hour, and it shows a minor master of the essay at her best.
12189-jim-waring-of-sonora-town-or-tang-:
Henry Herbert Knibbs published this western novel in August 1918, with verse prologues and illustrations by E. Boyd Smith. Jim Waring, a cowboy hero of Sonora Town, rides a desert borderland where outlaws, ranchers, and old grudges meet.

The plot opens with Waring ambushed by a Chola outlaw and builds through a silver crucifix, a horse trade, a murder hunt, and a fight in the open. Waring must decide whether to take revenge or trust a stubborn inner voice that warns him off killing. Knibbs writes in a mix of plain prose and cowboy ballad, full of desert light and dry humor. The novel belongs to the romantic western of its era, where honor is tested at gunpoint.
12290-the-church-and-modern-life:
Washington Gladden published The Church and Modern Life in 1908, a book of lectures on how American churches should meet a changing age. Gladden, a Congregational minister and social gospel leader, writes for church members, not scholars.

Chapters treat the roots of religion, other religions, the social side of faith, the business of the church, and the question whether the church is decadent. Later chapters argue for a coming reformation, social redemption, a new evangelism, and new leadership. Gladden defends trial by evidence over trial by ordeal, and reform over retreat. The book captures Progressive-era liberal Protestantism: hopeful, practical, and eager to join faith to public good.
12311-christ-the-way-the-truth-and-the-l:
The Reverend John Brown, minister at Wamphray, wrote Christ the Way, the Truth, and the Life during banishment in Holland. Brown, a seventeenth-century Scottish Covenanter, addresses believers suffering for conscience.

The book takes John chapter fourteen, verse six, as text: no man comes to the Father but by Christ. Chapters explain the words in general, then guide the believer kept from turning back on the way of God, still looking Zion-ward though progress is slow. Brown writes with pastoral care, urging prayer, patience, and trust. The work is a classic of Puritan devotion, valued for its plain counsel to persecuted Christians.
12759-the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-04-:
By Washington Gladden in 1904, under series editor Bliss Carman, this fourth volume of The World's Best Poetry gathers verse on religion and the higher life. Bryant, Gallagher, Bolton, and many others appear, with permissions noted from leading publishers. The series as a whole spans home, love, sorrow, nature, and national spirit across ten volumes.

Poems of convent gardens, moonlit olive trees, and a soul awaiting its heavenly spouse show the volume's devout, meditative tone. A heart hushed before a holy presence recurs as an image. The book suits readers who want classic religious verse in one well-chosen set.
12765-geordie-s-tryst-a-tale-of-scottish:
Attributed to Mrs. Milne Rae, Geordie's Tryst is a Scottish tale centred on Grace Campbell of Kirklands and a herd boy named Geordie. On a chilly spring day Grace walks out against advice to find the boy, and soon takes a keen interest in his schooling. Old Adam the gardener, Aunt Hume, and the minister Mr. Graham people the parish world.

Grace hurries home glowing to tell how she found Geordie, and the story follows their lessons, pride, and growing bond. The tale treats kindness across class lines with gentle moral warmth. Readers of Victorian Scottish fiction will find a modest, charming parish story.
13449-the-plain-man-and-his-wife:
Arnold Bennett writes for the plain man, meaning almost every man, rich and poor, idle and diligent, who wakes to another day as a grind. Chapters on all means and no end, the taste for pleasure, the risks of life. In her place follow one man's struggle to enjoy life while saving for a future that always recedes.

A man of thirty, told he would be no nearer happiness at forty-five with wife, family, and rising income, would smile in disbelief, Bennett says, yet that is the common fate. Chauffeurs, microbes, debts, and death remind the reader that life is short and risky. Bennett's counsel is plain: take pleasure now, do not sacrifice the present wholly to tomorrow.
13467-study-of-child-life:
Marion Foster Washburne's Study of Child Life, in the Library of Home Economics, treats child-rearing as a new profession of home-making. Prepared by teachers of recognised authority for mothers, teachers, physicians, nurses, and house managers, the course applies recent advances in arts and sciences to home, health, economy, and children.

Washburne studies the child's sense of fairness, as in the irritating reply, well, you do it yourself, and the ugly spirit that turns a true statement into an attack. She defends fairy tales as inside truth, told in the pigments of imagination, and advises parents to answer yes without hesitation when children ask if a story is true. The book blends psychology with practical home counsel.
13493-the-american-frugal-housewife:
Lydia Maria Child, writing in 1832 as Mrs. Child, dedicates this housekeeping manual to those not ashamed of economy. Franklin's line opens it: a fat kitchen makes a lean will, and economy is a poor man's revenue. Child gives the plain rules of a thrifty American home in the age before ready-made goods.

Mutton, pork, and veal cuts are pictured and named, bread and yeast are made at home, and ovens are seasoned by burning wood and raking coals. Dyes from purple sugar paper, white maple bark, and gum arabic colour stockings in slate shades. The book teaches cooking, cleaning, mending, and saving as household virtues, with thrift treated as sense, not meanness.
13572-the-son-of-clemenceau-a-novel-of-m:
Alexander Dumas fils writes The Son of Clemenceau, a sequel to The Clemenceau Case, as a novel of modern love and life. It opens at Munich in March weather, where. The sunset gun has fired from ramparts and a lonely wanderer winds his cloak against a chill breeze over the plain where the Isar flows darkly.

Munich, city of monks and realm of rheumatism, shows its unfashionable southern suburb of quaint structures, while the new town might justify the name German Athens. A woman holds out her hand to a man no longer her foe, praising a conversion that made a heartless libertine a true gentleman. Hedwig shudders at a vanished man's fate, said in a singular tone. Dumas writes love, honour, and mystery in a European key.
13739-shandygaff-a-number-of-most-agreea:
Christopher Morley called Shandygaff a set of agreeable inquiries upon life and letters, mixed with stories and skits. Published in 1918, it gathers essays on books, reading rooms, writers, and city life. Morley jokes about titles, dedications, and the British Museum washroom. He praises Gissing, London streets, and the habits of working writers.

Short stories break up the essays with humour and surprise. Morley writes as a friendly guide, never as a lecturer. He loves bookshops, libraries, and the small rituals of readers. The pieces are short enough to read one at a time. Together they give a warm portrait of literary life during wartime. The title drink, shandygaff, sets the light tone.
13970-nick-of-the-woods-or-adventures-of:
Robert M. Bird wrote Nick of the Woods, a frontier novel of prairie life in Kentucky. Bird's preface rejects the romantic Indian of Chateaubriand and Cooper, the noble savage of popular fancy. He presents Native peoples and settlers in harsher, more violent terms. Hunters in blanket coats and fringed hunting frocks fill the opening scenes.

The title figure, Nick, hunts through woods and prairies with grim purpose. Settlers, soldiers, and Native warriors clash over land and revenge. Bird's prose mixes adventure with debate about the frontier myth. Modern readers will note its period prejudices. The novel remains important for American frontier fiction and its critics.
1403-a-start-in-life:
Balzac's novel follows Oscar Husson, a restless young man from a modest Paris home, as he sets out to earn his living. A coach ride to the country, full of boasts and loose talk, lands him in trouble before his first post begins. His early career becomes a lesson in how small vanities can spoil large hopes.

Through clerks, lawyers, and family friends, Oscar learns the value of silence, steady work, and plain dealing. The book watches a youth grow into a man of business by slow steps and hard knocks. It is a kind but unsparing tale of ambition, gossip, and second chances.
14196-the-nervous-housewife:
Abraham Myerson, a Boston physician, published The Nervous Housewife in 1920, asking how old the problem truly is. Chapters define nervousness, sort housewives predisposed to it, and weigh housework, poverty, husbands, household conflicts, and symptoms used as weapons. Case histories and treatment close the book, with a final chapter on the future of woman, home, and marriage.

Disagreement, not idleness, drives the neurosis, Myerson argues. Housework may be menial, monotonous, and sedentary, yet it also offers privacy, individuality, and virtues civilization needs. Novelists and statesmen praise those agreeable phases enough already. What matters is what each woman finds disagreeable, how it works on her, and what to do about it. One patient, told bluntly that health depended on purpose and reason, improved greatly and returned to normal life. Medical, social, and frank, the book speaks to a new century's homes.
14204-the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-:
Charles Klein's Lion and the Mouse, novelized from his play by Arthur Hornblow in 1906, stages American power and pity. Judge Rossmore, tangled in scandal, retreats with his daughter Shirley toward Massapequa, where baseball teams, tea parties, and pinochle clubs fill local talk. New arrivals puzzle villagers who read only home hints, health articles, and fashions.

Shirley's plea gives the book its title image. Go to Washington and save my father's life, the frontispiece urges, as the mouse confronts the lion of railroad and senate power. Jefferson, a young man in the story, traps an English secretary named Bagley by copying a letter and springing exposure at a rendezvous. Judges and senators may be bought for gold, Pope's motto insists, but love and esteem never sell. Melodrama with a conscience, written for a popular stage age.
14213-three-months-of-my-life:
J. F. Foster, assistant-surgeon of Her Majesty's 36th Foot, kept this diary of three months in India and Kashmir, edited by Lizzie A. Freeth in 1873. Foster warns that hurry left spelling mistakes his relations could not all correct, and the rough edges remain. Gratitude opens the book: mercy preserved him through years in India and brought him home to all but one of those dear to him.

Travel detail fills the diary. Chepatties pass between khitmutgars' fingers, toasted and eaten dirt and all, while chicken appears at every meal, curried, roasted, or in soup, stringy as hemp and tough as a sandal. At Atchibul, twelve miles on, Foster takes a pavilion, sets fountains playing, and plays Great Mogul. A small black and yellow bird, called bulbul by his boatman, sings beside him in a cage. Birthday thoughts close the run, modest and homesick.
14357-rudolph-eucken-a-philosophy-of-lif:
Abel J. Jones wrote this study of Rudolf Eucken, a thinker who sought a philosophy of life. Jones, once of Jena and Cambridge, sets out Eucken's problem plainly. The book asks whether life has a meaning that facts cannot give. It moves from old answers to a new search for truth, and from past and present to the eternal. Religion, freedom, and the self stand at the center of the argument.

Jones tests logic with a case: if Carlo is an animal by steps, the end holds when the premises hold. He notes that premises drawn from science carry the same doubt as science itself. Later chapters trace the rise to freedom and personality, and the growth of a religion that is inward and real. Eucken calls the ripe form Characteristic Religion, a life drawn from a universal spiritual life. The book ends with criticism and praise in measure.
14373-a-noble-life:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's novel centers on the last Earl of Cairnforth, a Scottish nobleman whose title dies with him. Born to a great estate in the far north, he grows up under guardians and learns the duties his lands impose.

Helen, a devoted companion, and the people of the estate shape his choices as he faces poverty among tenants, family pride, and his own failing health. Craik presents his quiet service as true heroism, opposed to showy courage. The novel is a sentimental Victorian tale of duty, faith, and a life spent well.
14422-the-promise-of-american-life:
Herbert Croly's 1909 political study asks what American democracy was meant to achieve, and what it still owed its citizens. Croly, a New York journalist, traced the idea from the founding generation through party strife, slavery, and industrial growth.

He argues that Jefferson's faith in small government and Hamilton's faith in national power each captured only half the promise. Neither founder, in his view, foresaw industrial America. Croly instead urged a strong national state guided by democratic aims, able to curb trusts and widen opportunity. The book shaped Progressive debate, and later reformers drew on its call for planned national purpose.
14696-the-wheel-of-life:
Ellen Glasgow's 1906 novel follows a Virginia circle caught between old-fashioned feeling and a newer, more restless spirit. Its chapters promise a romantic hero who never quite arrives, an eccentric family, masques and mummeries, and a young man dreaming dreams.

Impulse gives way to pleasure, pursuit and retreat. A poor lover may prove an excellent friend, a lie may serve truth better than candour, and attraction between opposites brings danger as well as delight. Glasgow watches manners change without scolding her people, and the wheel of the title turns on choice: what a life gains when feeling, ambition and loyalty pull in different directions.
14963-the-world-as-i-have-found-it-seque:
Mary L. Day Arms, a blind author, writes The World as I Have Found It. It is a sequel to Incidents in the Life of a Blind Girl, published in Baltimore in 1878, with an introduction by the Reverend Charles F. Deems. Deems notes the title page shows the writer is blind, and that the first volume was widely sold.

Readers who followed that book will, he is sure, welcome its sequel. Arms tells how she navigates a sighted world, learns, works and keeps faith, with the plain detail of daily life carrying the argument. The memoir stands as an early American account of blindness written from inside, practical, devout and determined not to ask for pity.
15247-john-henry-smith-a-humorous-romanc:
Frederick Upham Adams's 1905 humorous romance presents John Henry Smith's diary, revised and edited by the author at Smith's request. Smith, abroad at the time, asked that marked passages be cut and others disguised to hide real people. Adams renamed characters but left their portraits as Smith drew them.

Outdoor life, golf, fishing, and social comedy fill the diary, with sketches by A. B. Frost to match. The book is dedicated to Adams's daughter Olive Marie. Readers who enjoy light Edwardian humor will find John Henry Smith funny, breezy, and full of sporting charm.
15424-ella-barnwell-a-historical-romance:
Emerson Bennett published this historical romance of border life in Cincinnati in 1853, in a revised edition. His preface states the design plainly: blend fact and fiction to picture the dress, customs, and warlike habits of early western pioneers, while telling a story that moves to its proper end. Kentucky in its infancy is the scene, and its early settlement records were read and compared for the tale.

The heroine Ella Barnwell moves among frontier households, where strangers, teasing, and sudden laughter fill domestic scenes, and where the Revolutionary struggle presses on the border. Bennett mixes love story with frontier history, giving readers both a heroine and a chronicle of settlement. The novel shows mid-century America's taste for history as romance: true events, dressed in fiction, to teach how the West was won.
15588-the-pilot-and-his-wife:
Jonas Lie's Norwegian novel, translated by G. L. Tottenham, appeared with William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London in 1877. The opening sets the scene on Norway's stern, pine-clad southern coast, off Arendal. There the white walls of the Great and Little Torungen lighthouses stand far out at sea. Each stands on its bare rock island. Spray drives against the walls in storms, and sea-birds dash themselves against the glass at night.

Winter often cuts all communication with land, by drift or patchy ice, impassable on foot or by boat. These lights are of recent erection; many living readers remember when the gleam of white breakers was the only lighting for long reaches. Lie writes a sea novel of pilots, lighthouse keepers, and their wives, where isolation, storms, and duty shape a marriage on a dangerous coast.
15610-first-love-and-other-fascinating-s:
This Little Blue Book, number 1195, edited by E. Haldeman-Julius in Girard, Kansas, gathers five fascinating stories of Spanish life. Emilia Pardo-Bazán opens with First Love. Serafín Estébanez Calderón follows with an Andalusian duel, and Juan Eugenio Hartzenbusch with Mariquita the Bald. Armando Palacio Valdés adds the love of Clotilde, and Pedro Antonio de Alarcón adds Captain Veneno's proposal of marriage.

First Love opens with a narrator unsure of age, eleven or twelve, more probably thirteen, since southern hearts mature early. He slips into his aunt's bedroom while she is at church, rummaging drawers that serve as a museum of sandalwood fans, faded satin pin cushions, and knitted mittens. The stories mix romance, duel, and comedy, in short, vivid Spanish tales made cheap and handy for American readers.
15738-married-life:
A 1920 novel of marriage by May Edginton, issued in Boston by Small, Maynard and Company. Edginton dedicates the book, in admiration, to a completely successful husband. Her chapters trace a marriage from anticipation to separation and home-coming. The novel treats love after the wedding, not before it.

Anticipation, housekeeping, discipline, and disillusion follow in turn, with a baby, problems, and recrimination. A banged door, drifting, and intrigue test the bond, before plain dealing and revival offer hope. Edginton writes with frank, modern sympathy for both partners. The book reads as an honest novel of married life: tender at first, hard in the middle, and wise at the end.
1586-man-and-wife:
Wilkie Collins's Man and Wife opens with a prologue, The Irish Marriage, in a villa at Hampstead. Then moves to a ship bound from Gravesend to Bombay, where two eighteen-year-old girls weep bitterly in a cabin. Their story becomes a novel about marriage law, sport, and a wife's rights in Victorian England.

Through Scottish marriages, athletic contests, and a husband's cruelty, Collins argues against laws that trapped women in bad marriages. The novel is long and polemical. It is a characteristic Collins blend of sensation and social protest, full of legal traps and determined heroines.
1588-a-rogue-s-life:
Wilkie Collins's Rogue's Life, written more than twenty years before its book form and first published in Household Words, follows a rogue's career in the author's early manner. Collins delayed republication at a friend's suggestion, and the book at last gathers the rogue's adventures, from petty crime to larger schemes, with humour and verve.

The rogue narrates his own rise and fall, and Collins enjoys his company's wit even while condemning his trade. The tale is short and brisk. A Rogue's Life is a pleasant early Collins work, a warm-up for the sensation novels that made his name.
15895-allegories-of-life:
A book of allegories by Mrs. J. S. Adams, issued in 1872. Twenty-three short pieces teach moral lessons through pictures from daily life. Adams writes in plain, earnest prose for family reading. Each allegory stands alone, yet all point one way: upward.

The Bells opens in an old church steeple, where a beautiful chime rings joyous peals for years. The Height, The Pilgrim, Faith, Hope, and Joy and Sorrow follow, with The Oak, Truth and Error, and The Two Ways. Self-exertion, The Vines, The Feast, and The Sacrifice close the set. The book offers Victorian moral teaching at its gentlest: stories that preach by image, not by scolding.
16340-a-cynic-looks-at-life:
Ambrose Bierce turns his sharp pen on civilization itself in this short book, reprinted as Little Blue Book No. 1099 in 1912. The opening essay asks whether civilization truly civilizes, and finds the question dodging its own point. Later pieces take up travelers' tales, human nature, and the gap between fine words and real conduct.

Bierce writes in short, biting paragraphs, with wit that cuts both ways. No party or creed escapes his eye. The book is brief enough for one sitting, but its barbs linger. Readers who like satire with teeth will find it a classic sample of Bierce at his most sardonic.
16943-paris-with-pen-and-pencil-its-peop:
David W. Bartlett built this Paris portrait from two stays in the city, one while Louis Napoleon led the Republic and one after he became emperor. He does not offer a route book for tourists. Instead he sketches streets, churches, the Louvre, gardens, tombs, prisons, and markets, and he adds short studies of Paris figures.

Lamartine, Hugo, Dumas, George Sand, Guizot, and Thiers all appear among the sketches, along with notes on French writers of earlier days. The mix gives a plain sense of how Paris looked, how its people lived, and why its books mattered to its fame. Readers who want the feel of mid-1800s Paris, not just its sights, will find it here in clear, firsthand scenes.
16959-way-down-east-a-romance-of-new-eng:
Joseph R. Grismer wrote this romance of New England life, founded on Lottie Blair Parker's very successful play of the same title. Grosset and Dunlap issued it in New York in 1900 with stills from D. W. Griffith's film. Anna Moore, played by Lillian Gish in the film, stands at its heart. Chapters run from a conquering hero and a mock marriage, through desolation, mother and daughter, village gossip, and David's confession of love.

Grismer tells of a wronged girl, a stern village, and love that wins through scandal and snow. The tale mixes stage melodrama with New England farm life. Readers who like old melodramas will find a moving, moral story, famous in its day on stage and screen alike.
17146-diddie-dumps-tot-or-plantation-chi:
Louise-Clarke Pyrnelle's 1882 book, dedicated to her father of Selma, Alabama, tells plantation child life through Diddie, Dumps, and Tot. Chapters cover Christmas on the old plantation, Mammy's story, Old Billy, Uncle Snake-bit Bob's Sunday school, plantation games, and a meeting with Uncle Daniel's sermon. The preface states her aim: to keep old stories, games, hymns, and tales of enslaved Black folk alive.

Pyrnelle writes from a slaveholder family's view, praising pleasant ties between master and slave, a frame modern readers should approach with care. The tales, games, and songs themselves hold folk value. Readers of Southern folk life will find a rich, if deeply dated, record of plantation childhood and Black story tradition.
17246-the-quest-of-the-simple-life:
W. J. Dawson's 1907 book tells how a Londoner of many years, torn between paradise and a house of bondage in the city, sought a simpler life in the country. Chapters move from getting a living and earth hunger to health and money, a search for the picturesque, and at last a cottage of his own. Buying happiness, how they lived, and neighborship fill the middle of the quest.

Dawson loves London yet longs for green fields, a tension he states with honesty and humor. His tale is part memoir, part advice on plain living, and it ends by asking if he was right. Readers weary of city rush will find a gentle, thoughtful pioneer of the simple-life movement.
17259-his-second-wife:
Ernest Poole's His Second Wife opens on a train to New York, where two young women face each other in a parlor car, deep in talk. Fellow riders guess their ages at twenty-two and thirty and take them for sisters, though the blonde looks sleek and moneyed while the brunette is slim, dark, and eager. The little lady's firm verdict, family resemblance, sets up the tale's puzzle.

Poole follows the pair through love, marriage, and the tangles of a second wife's place in a new home. His prose is observant and modern for its day, keen on looks, talk, and social masks. Readers who like early-1900s novels of marriage and manners will find a thoughtful, well-drawn story here.
17532-two-knapsacks-a-novel-of-canadian-:
J. Cawdor Bell wrote this novel of Canadian summer life, published in Toronto by the Williamson Book Company and entered in 1892 under the Parliament of Canada. Its heroes, Eugene Coristine and Farquhar Wilkinson, are youngish bachelors and fellow members of the Victoria and Albert Literary Society, where they debate, read essays, and print a manuscript magazine. Their summer trip gives the book its shape.

Chapters head for the Queen's Wharf, the Northern Railway, Belle Ewart, and the steamer Susan Thomas, with a musical performance, a sly dog, a misunderstanding, and Kempenfeldt Bay along the way. Readers get a light Canadian summer novel, full of literary talk, travel, and humour. It offers a pleasant view of Ontario holiday life in the 1890s.
17617-david-harum-a-story-of-american-li:
Edward Noyes Westcott published this story of American life in New York in 1899 with D. Appleton and Company, copyright dated 1898. His introduction argues that contemporary native fiction increasingly sets plot aside in favour of bold, realistic portraits of American types and manners. David Harum, the shrewd countryman at the centre, embodies that fashion.

Readers meet a small-town world of horse dealing, banking, and neighbourly talk, told through Harum's own sharp sayings. The novel became a popular success and a stage favourite in its day. It suits readers of American local colour and of the character novel, where one strong figure carries the book.
17780-scenes-of-clerical-life:
George Eliot wrote Scenes of Clerical Life as her first fiction, printed here in Everyman's Library, first issued in 1910. The book holds three long tales of country clergy in the English Midlands, told with the keen eye that would soon make Eliot famous.

The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton opens the set, with a plain parson, a shabby church, and pews kept for local gentry. Mr. Gilfil's Love Story and Janet's Repentance follow, on love, drink, and grace. Eliot writes with warmth and irony, and the tales still charm as portraits of small-town faith, folly, and kind hearts.
1821-a-charmed-life:
Richard Harding Davis opens with a woman who loves a war correspondent named Chesterton so much that when he leaves for a little war she cannot understand or quite forgive him. Chesterton has watched other wars from the sidelines, but this time he rides at a gallop toward men lying in ambush. The report of rifles becomes the signal for a massacre on the hill above.

The story follows love under the strain of war reporting, and Davis writes it with the knowledge of a man who had been there himself. Its title is ironic: the charmed life is the one the correspondent believes he leads, until the moment when charm runs out and the guns begin.
18335-the-breath-of-life:
John Burroughs published this book of nature essays in May 1915. Burroughs, a well-known American naturalist, takes up the oldest question in his field: what life itself is, and how it differs from mere matter. His opening finds him hoeing burdocks at the edge of his garden and asking what force drives their lusty growth.

Chapters treat the living wave, a wonderful world, the baffling problem, scientific vitalism, life and mind, life and science, the journeying atoms, and the vital order. Burroughs weighs science against wonder without giving up either. Readers get a naturalist's meditation, plain and personal, on why living things grow, move, and pass, and what science can and cannot say about them.
18584-the-edge-of-the-knife:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science-fiction story for Amazing Stories in May 1957. The editors noted that two top-flight editors had rejected it as too hot to handle and too dangerous for their books. The story asks readers to judge whether that warning was fair.

The opening finds teacher Chalmers stopped mid-talk by his class's sudden attention, as a pupil asks about the assassination of Khalid ib'n Hussein at Basra in 1973. The tale turns on a classroom lesson that slips across time, where a great chaotic now replaces past and future, and where a single killing changes what comes next.
18708-dr-dumany-s-wife:
Maurus Jókai's novel, translated from the Hungarian by F. Steinitz and published by Doubleday, Page in 1891, begins on a St. Gothard train near the close of 1876. Its narrator, bound for Paris, finds the sleeping cars full and buys his berth with a large tip, and the story that follows spans two parts.

Early chapters introduce a dumb child, a dark god, an Englishman, a nabob, and a republican countess, before reaching Dumany Kornel himself. The second part moves through a sea-dove, a four-leaved clover, a brilliant game, and a search for death toward light at last. The book blends travel, romance, and mystery in the manner of Hungary's best-known storyteller of the day.
18875-the-prairie-wife:
Arthur Stringer published this novel in 1915, by arrangement with Bobbs-Merrill, with a color frontispiece by H. T. Dunn. The table of contents is arranged by days, beginning Thursday the Nineteenth, giving the book the feel of a dated record kept on the prairie. The frontispiece shows a trap-door scene, with a cry to get down quickly.

The story follows life on the open plains: farm work, weather, neighbors, and the strains and pleasures of a household far from town. Stringer writes with a Westerner's eye for landscape and daily labor. Readers get a prairie novel of the settlement era, told in close, dated episodes that build a picture of frontier married life.
19946-villa-elsa-a-story-of-german-famil:
Villa Elsa calls itself a story of German family life. It opens in late summer 1913 with an American in Germany. He is a quiet college man of twenty-three, tall and lean. He has been idling on a trip without thought of adventure. He observes his surroundings without being observed, at first. Stuart Henry framed German domestic life for American readers. War was one summer away from that idyll.

American travel writers explained Germany to a curious republic. Family life made a nation legible to foreign guests. Henry's young observer drifts into the household of Villa Elsa. What he learns is the book's real plot. Read now, the calm of 1913 feels ominous. The novel preserves that last prewar summer.
20287-a-night-in-the-snow-or-a-struggle-:
A Night in the Snow, or A Struggle for Life, tells of peril in deep winter. The writer speaks of himself in a very personal manner throughout. He saw no way to give the facts without that frank approach. His duties and the country he crossed must be described firsthand.

Geography lies at the heart of this tale of snow and survival. A night exposed in such cold can kill in a few hours. The struggle of the title pits one man against storm and drift. Readers get a stark, personal record of endurance in a frozen land.
21036-my-friend-smith-a-story-of-school-:
At twelve, the teller of My Friend Smith is shipped from Brownstroke village without clear cause. Stonebridge House, an academy for backward and troublesome young gentlemen, awaits him near Cliffshire. Talbot Baines Reed opens his tale of school and city life on that exile.

Smith, the friend of the title, anchors the tale's trials and triumphs. School scrapes give way to city work, want, and hard-won rise. Reed blends his school craft with a Dickens-like city warmth here. The book ranks among his best-loved, proof that his honest, hopeful tales could grip far past the school gate.
21043-reginald-cruden-a-tale-of-city-lif:
Heat drives even Squires, the lodge keeper, to nap in his coolest nook in Reginald Cruden. Lads might take any liberty with his garden while he sleeps so sweetly. Talbot Baines Reed opens his tale of city life on that drowsy gate.

Reginald, a school lad turned city clerk, meets London's grind and glitter head-on. Want, pride, true friends, and false ones mark his climb from low rooms. Reed Dickens-like warmth for young strivers fills the book's best pages. Reginald Cruden stands among his most loved city tales, a school story grown up and set down in London's hard streets.
21045-education-and-the-higher-life:
Sacred hours when we claim the love of higher things fill Education and the Higher Life. The essayist holds that faith and hope make mortal life immortal there. A moment so filled, he writes, holds wealth that lasts through years.

Essays here urge schools to train souls, not just minds stuffed with facts. The higher life of the title means faith, taste, and moral reach. Such writing served teachers who feared mere exam craft in schools. Readers meet Victorian education thought at its most earnest, keen to wed learning to a life of depth and worth.
21137-parkhurst-boys-and-other-stories-o:
Talbot Baines Reed, the master of the school story, gathers four groups of tales in this volume. Seven Parkhurst sketches cover matches, boat races, and school events, starting with a first football match and a coveted place in the fifteen. Eleven short pieces describe types of boys, such as the Sneak.

Twelve more stories retell boys from English history, including the Princes in the Tower, Dick Whittington, and Edward the Sixth. Seven longer general stories close the book. Reed wrote for the Boy's Own Paper world, and these pieces show his range: sport, humour, history, and schoolboy character in turn.
21432-aunt-judith-the-story-of-a-loving-:
Grace Beaumont tells a schoolgirl's tale in Aunt Judith, the story of a loving life, first published in 1888. Winnifred Blake bursts into the schoolroom with news at the start. A quarrel among the girls sets the plot in motion.

At its heart stands Aunt Judith, whose talks guide Winnie and her friends. Chapters move through a Christmas party, a sailor boy, a prize essay, and gathering clouds. Choices about truth, pride, and kindness drive each turn. The tale ends in light after darkness, true to its aim. It is a warm specimen of the moral girls' story of its age.
21840-woman-her-sex-and-love-life:
Plain medical counsel for women fills this 1917 book by William J. Robinson, a New York doctor and editor of journals on urology and sexology. Robinson had written many works on sexual health, eugenics, and marriage, and edited The Critic and Guide. Here he addresses women directly on their bodies, their marriages, and their love lives. Such frankness was bold in print at the time.

The book belongs to the early fight for open sex education in America. Robinson believed ignorance, not knowledge, did the harm. He writes in a doctor's plain voice, case by case and topic by topic. Modern readers will find some views dated and others strikingly fresh. As a record of what one reforming physician dared to print in 1917, it holds its place.
22233-blazed-trail-stories-and-stories-o:
Stewart Edward White published Blazed Trail Stories and Stories of the Wild Life in 1904. White had worked in Michigan lumber camps and hunted across the continent. His title set collects tales from his popular novel The Blazed Trail and from his years in the woods. The opening story fills a lumber town's sawdust streets with Sunday crowds.

Loggers in stiff Sunday best escort their wives and sweethearts; outsiders try not to look conspicuous. White knew this world from inside and wrote it without romance or contempt. His animal stories rest on the same close watching. Few American writers of 1904 could match his record of the vanishing lumber frontier.
22295-on-prayer-and-the-contemplative-li:
On Prayer and the Contemplative Life gathers writings of St. Thomas Aquinas on the life of prayer. Its opening pages reach Aquinas's death at the abbey of Fossa Nuova. At the gates he quoted the psalm: his rest was there for ever, and there he would dwell, for he had chosen it. The great schoolman died there in 1274, worn out on a journey to a council.

The treatise that follows draws his teaching from the Summa and his commentaries. Prayer, contemplation, and the active life are weighed and ordered. Hugh Pope, the Dominican editor, made the volume for English readers. It shows the angel of the schools as a man of prayer, not only of argument.
22411-the-choice-of-life:
Georgette Leblanc wrote The Choice of Life, published in 1914. Leblanc was a French actress and writer of strong, searching temperament. Her book opens with questions she cannot shake off or answer.

Is anything definite, she asks, amid blind efforts and impulses? Since her first awakening, urges have pushed her toward other women. What had she wanted from them all that time? She stretched out her hands and searched their hearts. At times she changed the very nature of their strivings. The book pursues those questions as a spiritual autobiography. Readers meet a woman examining love, art, and freedom without flinching.
22432-parables-of-the-christ-life:
I. Lilias Trotter wrote Parables of the Christ-Life, a devotional book of plant parables. Trotter was a missionary and artist with a gift for nature imagery. Her starting text is Christ's word on being born again.

Except a man be born again, he cannot see God's kingdom. Every soul, Trotter writes, carries a possible second life. Like a flower, it holds more than its first birth shows. To souls within the Gospel's reach, a moment of receiving comes. The Life of God draws near and could be received if willing. From flowers and seeds she draws those lessons. Readers get gentle, pictured teaching on spiritual growth.
2271-he-fell-in-love-with-his-wife:
Edward P. Roe's novel takes a broken marriage and asks whether love can be learned a second time. He Fell in Love with His Wife follows a husband who, after years of coldness, sets out to court his own wife as if she were a stranger. He hopes to win back what habit and neglect destroyed. The rural setting gives the courtship room to breathe.

Roe, a popular minister-novelist, writes plainly about forgiveness, patience, and the daily work of affection. The story's charm lies in its sincerity rather than its surprise. Readers who enjoy gentle domestic fiction will find a warm, old-fashioned romance.
22839-jesse-cliffe:
London at dusk glows in Jesse Cliffe, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. One voice praises the prospect from Waterloo Bridge on a summer evening above all London sights. Sunset tints reflect in the Thames below. Later, lamps and boat lights blend with soft moonlight on the river.

Mitford usually writes of villages, so the city setting marks a change of air. The story carries its people between the worlds she knew, town brightness and country quiet. Talk, scenery, and character do the work that plot does in louder tales. Readers who know her through Our Village will enjoy seeing the same fond, precise eye turned on the Thames and its evening crowds.
23092-the-simple-life:
Wedding chaos crowds The Simple Life, dated 1901 in this edition. Congratulations, acceptances, and refusals pile up from attendants, alongside tradesmen's excuses. Last-minute disasters follow. A death scrambles the bridal party, and a bad cold silences the favorite singer. They will never be ready, though they thought they had foreseen everything.

Charles Wagner's plea for simpler living found millions of readers, and scenes like this wedding explain why. Modern ceremony, shopping, and display had already begun to crush the occasions they decorated. Wagner, a French pastor, writes with warmth rather than scolding. His simple life is not poverty but proportion, and the bridal panic makes his case better than any sermon.
23172-the-damned-thing-1898-from-in-the-:
Ambrose Bierce reads a dead man's diary in The Damned Thing, dated 1898, from In the Midst of Life. One reader at the inquest stands out a little, the scene notes. A man of the world, plainly, though something in his dress ties him to the wild country around him.

That dry, scientific diction is Bierce preparing his trap. A coroner's jury, a mutilated body, and a diary that blames something the eye cannot register make this his most famous horror tale. The damned thing itself stays exactly where Bierce put it, just outside human senses. Few American stories have been imitated so often, or matched so rarely. The inquest's calm procedure makes the conclusion colder than any scream.
2505-the-heir-of-redclyffe:
Charlotte Yonge's Heir of Redclyffe follows Guy Morville, a young heir with a violent temper, who struggles to master himself under the guidance of his cousin Philip and the woman he loves. The novel's tragedy and redemption made it one of the great Victorian bestsellers, shaping a generation's ideals of honor and self-control. Yonge writes with High Church earnestness and deep feeling.

The story's power lies in Guy's slow, painful growth and in the love that sustains him. Modern readers will find its morals intense but its hero unforgettable. It remains a landmark of Victorian domestic fiction.
2601-heartsease-or-the-brother-s-wife:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this long Victorian novel of a family tested by love, duty, and a brother's marriage. The heroine enters a house where a brother's wife must find her place among proud kin, and the sunlit park of the opening soon gives way to harder weather.

Yonge follows her characters through illness, misunderstanding, and quiet acts of faith, in the earnest style her readers loved. The title flower, love in idleness, hints at passions that bloom where they should not. The book offers a patient portrait of domestic honor, and of women holding a family together.
2727-allan-s-wife:
H. Rider Haggard tells Allan Quatermain's early days in this romance, from a fire fight and a march northwards to the Zulu impi and the end of a laager. Stella enters the story, then a baboon woman, marble kraals, and a plea to go in, Allan, that drives the plot.

Hendrika plots evil, a loved one vanishes, and the magic of Indaba Zimbi shapes what happens to Stella across fifteen chapters and more. Haggard writes with his usual pace and African color. The book serves as a prequel to Quatermain's later fame, and a tale of love in a hard land.
2778-jewel-a-chapter-in-her-life:
Clara Louise Burnham wrote this story of Jewel, a girl whose life changes when a new coachman arrives and a Chicago letter comes. Mother and daughter, father and son, and a bon voyage carry Jewel from one household to another, in the 1903 Grosset and Dunlap edition.

Jewel's goodness, faith, and pluck soften the grown ups around her, in the sentimental style Burnham's readers loved. The book is offered in loving acknowledgment to its first inspiration. It charms as a wholesome tale of a child who heals a family by simply being herself.
2936-geological-contemporaneity-and-pers:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote Geological Contemporaneity and Persistent Types of Life as a stocktaking for science. He compares the scientist to a merchant who pauses after speculation, gain, and loss to count solid possessions. The man of science, he argues, should re-examine the common stock in trade and make sure how far the bullion in the cellar justifies the paper built on it. The essay then tests geological time against persistent forms of life.

Huxley insists that changes in life have taken place in a definite order, and that the statement of that order is what scientists call a natural law. Whether that law expresses natural forces or a supernatural power's chosen manner is secondary, so long as the order exists. The essay remains a clear statement of how geology and biology support each other.
3111-certain-diversities-of-american-lif:
Warner calls his an interesting age and proves it with measures of change. Within living memory, the trotting horse's mile fell from two minutes forty seconds to two minutes eight and a quarter. A boys' pastime of fifteen years earlier had grown into a great national industry. It was organized and professional, played for money that rivaled the Stock Exchange.

The game had ceased to be exercise for the many and become spectacle for the many. From such markers Warner builds a portrait of American life diversifying fast. New sports, new money, and new crowds fill the essay. It now reads as a snapshot of a country remaking its pace in a single generation.
3117-the-relation-of-literature-to-life:
Warner pairs a sketch of his own life with his title essay on books and living. Thomas R. Lounsbury wrote the sketch. It begins in Franklin County in northwestern Massachusetts, a land of romantic beauty. Farm families lived plainly there, roads were wretched save in summer, and stones were among the surest crops. Religion ran deep, culture came sparingly, and plain living outweighed high thinking.

Against that background Warner asks what books do for such a life. Literature, he argues, is a living force, not an ornament. It shapes conduct and judgment in ordinary places. The essay stays a plain-spoken case for why reading matters beyond school and salon.
3336-within-an-inch-of-his-life:
Emile Gaboriau, father of the French detective novel, opens this mystery with fire at Valpinson. The first part states its facts plainly. In the night from 22 to 23 June 1871, toward one in the morning, Sauveterre was startled by a furious gallop. Sauveterre was the principal and most densely populated suburb of that pretty town. A messenger rides through the dark with news of burning.

From that gallop Gaboriau builds a tale of murder, money, and mistaken identity, in which a man's life hangs on a thread of evidence. The plot tightens with each witness until a life hangs on a thread of evidence. Gaboriau's method, later borrowed by all, is here in full working order.
334-episodes-in-van-bibber-s-life:
Richard Harding Davis follows Van Bibber, a cheerful young man about town, through comic episodes. Episodes in Van Bibber's Life opens behind the scenes on the first night of a comic opera, The Sultana. Anxious actors, a wardrobe woman's son, and a calm hero fill the scene.

Later episodes give Van Bibber a man servant, a hungry man fed, and a dog loved for its mistress's sake. Davis writes New York society with humor and pace. Van Bibber's politeness never breaks, even on feverish nights. The stories made Davis a favorite of magazine readers.
3379-short-stories-and-essays-from-liter:
William Dean Howells gathers short stories and essays in this volume from Literature and Life. The contents run from worries of a winter walk and summer isles of Eden to wild flowers of the asphalt and a circus in the suburbs. A she Hamlet, the midnight platoon, and the beach at Rockaway follow, with sawdust in the arena and a visit to a dime museum.

American literature in exile, the horse show, and the problem of the summer continue the set, with aesthetic New York and fifty-odd years ago. From New York into New England and the art of the adsmith close the range the contents reveal. Together the pieces show Howells the observer at large: city and country, high art and low show, all noted with the same mild, exact eye.
3380-staccato-notes-of-a-vanished-summer:
William Dean Howells writes staccato notes of a vanished summer in this piece from Literature and Life. Monday afternoon opens it, with a storm beating against a southeasterly wind nearly all day. The storm thickened, fold upon fold, in the northwest, and the gale increased. It blackened the harbor and whitened the open sea beyond, where sail after sail appeared round the reef of Whaleback Light.

The sails ran in a wild scamper for safe harbor, and the notes follow them in short, sharp bursts. Howells writes summer as a thing already past, remembered in weather. The sea, the light, and the hurrying sails do the work of elegy for a summer already past.
3382-american-literary-centers-from-lite:
William Dean Howells asks where American literature lives in this essay from Literature and Life. Americans, he writes, find it hard to get an inattentive outside world to grasp one fact: we seem to possess our own literature, yet lack any literary capital. Our output is so large that even we sometimes feel sure a centre must exist.

We reasonably ask ourselves: if not here or there, where else could it be? Howells answers by scattering the map: Boston, New York, and the West all claim a share, and none holds the whole. A literature without a capital, made in many towns at once: Howells scatters the map and calls it honest.
3383-spanish-prisoners-of-war-from-liter:
William Dean Howells writes about an unexpected sight in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in this essay from Literature and Life. Two American cruisers, the St Louis and the Harvard, have brought in sixteen or seventeen hundred Spanish prisoners taken at Santiago de Cuba. Most are sailors and marines from Admiral Cervera's fleet, with some soldiers captured in the fighting on land.

Howells admits he has little taste for war, yet he is struck by the human scene on the shore. The prisoners are carried to an island up the river, where the tide runs hard through the Narrows. His account dwells on pity and curiosity rather than triumph, and it gives a civilian view of the Spanish American War far from the battlefield.
3384-some-anomalies-of-the-short-story-f:
William Dean Howells examines the short story's odd standing in this essay from Literature and Life. An experiment by a great publishing house prompts it. Several volumes of short stories went out serially, in the hope that courageous persistence may overcome popular indifference to such collections when severally administered. The hope suggests questions about the eldest form of fiction.

Why do readers love single stories and neglect books of them? Howells turns the puzzle over with his usual patience, weighing magazines, habit, and the story's own brevity. Readers and writers alike still recognize the puzzle: single stories loved, collections neglected. It is a classic statement of the short story's problem, still familiar, from the editor who published more good stories than almost any man of his age.
3385-last-days-in-a-dutch-hotel-from-lit:
William Dean Howells recalls a cold September week at Scheveningen, the Dutch seaside resort near The Hague, in this travel essay from Literature and Life. The hotel porter warns the party they will be cold, and he proves right. A steady wind blows for days, and barely a hundred guests rattle around halls built for five hundred.

The charm of the piece lies in its small observations. Howells watches bathers in the surf, notes the long shared tables, and studies how a grand hotel feels when the season has nearly ended. The essay suits readers who enjoy travel writing that cares more about mood, weather, and fellow guests than about sights checked off a list.
3387-confessions-of-a-summer-colonist-fr:
William Dean Howells writes as a summer visitor on the Down East coast of Maine in this essay from Literature and Life. The season is ending in the small settlement where he has spent three months, and he already feels homesick for it. He wants some form of words that will hold a likeness of the place through the winter.

The essay then records the fixed habits of colony life. Everyone dines between one and two and sups at seven, whether in hotel or cottage, and visiting follows its own strict clock. Howells treats these rules with fond humor. The piece gives a clear picture of how wealthy Americans spent summers by the sea before cars and air travel changed the coast.
3424-for-the-term-of-his-natural-life:
Marcus Clarke sets this grim novel in the convict system of colonial Australia. Its hero is transported for a crime he did not commit, and the book follows him from trial and the prison ship through years of labor, escape attempts, and punishment. Clarke says he drew on events that had actually happened, and he does not soften the cruelty of the system.

The novel's power lies in its scale. It shows convicts, guards, officials, and free settlers caught in one harsh machine, and it asks what such a life does to conscience and hope. Readers should expect a long, dark story, but also one of the classic Australian novels, still read for its force and its protest against transportation.
3470-such-is-life:
Joseph Furphy, writing as Tom Collins, sets this Australian novel among bullock drivers, farmers, and travelers in the Riverina country. The narrator, Tom Collins, records long conversations on the road, in camps, and at stations, mixing philosophy, jokes, and local gossip. The book has no tight plot; its life lies in talk and in the slow rhythm of work with teams and wagons.

Furphy writes in a rich, digressive style, full of Australian slang, Latin tags, and sudden asides. Beneath the humor runs a serious view of class, land, and mateship in colonial New South Wales. Such Is Life became a classic of Australian letters, and it suits patient readers who enjoy a novel that wanders like a road and thinks aloud as it goes.
3692-the-house-of-life:
Poet and painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti built this book as one long chain of sonnets on love, youth, and death. The poems move through first passion, parting, memory, and grief, with each fourteen line piece adding one more scene or thought to a larger story of a life in love. Rossetti, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite circle, wrote in rich, image heavy verse that treats the beloved as both a real woman and a symbol of art itself.

Readers meet sonnets on kisses and partings, on songs heard in dreams, and on the slow work of loss after love ends. Willowwood, the wood of weeping and forgetfulness, gives the book some of its darkest music. The sequence rewards slow reading, since single lines echo across poems written years apart, and the whole gains weight as joy gives way to mourning and then to calm.
4117-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-01-pre:
An introductory volume to Samuel Pepys's diary gives his life story and family background before the diary itself begins. Pepys, born in 1633 and dead in 1703, came from a family of six sons and five daughters, and rose from modest roots to the Navy Office.

The preface follows his appointment to the fleet that brought Charles the Second to Dover. Ships with names hateful to Royalists were renamed, and the king came aboard the Naseby on May 23. Readers meet the man behind the diary first, which makes the daily entries that follow read with far more force.
4225-first-and-last-things-a-confession-:
H. G. Wells's First and Last Things sets out a confession of faith and a rule of life for a modern mind. He watches people simplify life's confusion through vegetarian diet and scientific research, through excesses of self-discipline and devotion to one art, or through drugs and drink.

That desire to simplify, Wells argues, is essentially the religious motive, the search for a unity behind life's tangle. The book moves from belief to conduct, offering a personal creed without a church. Readers who like Wells the thinker will find a frank, searching self-portrait.
423-round-the-red-lamp-being-facts-and-f:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers medical tales round the red lamp that once marked a doctor's door in this volume. Stories follow young doctors, old surgeons, and patients through births, operations, and grim wards. Doyle warns in his preface that medical life shows both heroism and bitter sorrow, and he does not soften either.

Tales include a first operation, a straggler from Waterloo, a lady's strange case, and a mummy numbered Lot 249. Some chill, some move, all show doctors as flawed, striving folk. The book stands apart from Doyle's detective work, as a grave, humane look at healing and its costs.
4338-the-freedom-of-life:
Annie Payson Call, author of Power Through Repose, wrote this book on freedom as a matter of health, habit, and spirit. It opens with a hymn to the Lord God of Israel. The hymn prays for freedom from bondage, from alien minds, and from idols. It prays for the law to be kept in freedom rather than fear.

Call's counsel is gentle and practical. Rest, attention, and the giving up of strain form a path to a freer life. She writes for readers worn by nervous hurry, offering small changes of mind and body. The book belongs to the early twentieth-century literature of repose, and it keeps a devotional tone throughout.
4541-the-crown-of-life:
George Gissing published The Crown of Life in the mid-1880s world of London, opening at Waterloo Station on a May morning in 1886. Piers Otway, a slim, dark young man of twenty-one, steps from a suburban train in a silk hat and morning coat, yet he lacks the City countenance. He walks to Charing Cross and the Haymarket, where a picture shop window draws his eye past landscapes to the faces and forms of beautiful women.

From that wandering start grows a novel about art, love, and the search for a worthy life, as Piers weighs ambition against affection and the claims of family. Gissing writes with close London detail and a sober, reflective tone. Readers get a serious late-Victorian novel about a young man trying to crown his life with something better than money or show, and about the women and work that shape his choice.
4587-finger-posts-on-the-way-of-life:
T. S. Arthur published Finger Posts on the Way of Life in 1853, using a road sign as his image for moral guidance. His preface says life's path is new and strange to each traveller. It is often rough and thorny, winding through difficulty and danger, with a sky so dark that the narrow safe line is hard to see. This little book, he says, aims to point the wary traveller in the right direction.

Arthur does not claim the high mission of the preacher. Yet he never forgets that natural life exists for the sake of spiritual life, and that no one lives well who does not live for Heaven. The finger-posts therefore point both to safe walking through the world and to a higher end. Readers get a short set of Victorian conduct sketches, easy to dip into, meant to steady a reader on an ordinary day.
4597-eclectic-school-readings-stories-fr:
Orison Swett Marden, author of Architects of Fate and editor of Success, compiled Eclectic School Readings: Stories from Life as a book for young people. His preface states its aim plainly: to make a life, as well as to make a living, is one of the supreme objects for which we must all struggle. The sooner young readers grasp that, he says, the greater and more worthy the life they will make.

The volume gathers brief life stories and incidents from great lives, showing boys handicapped by poverty and discouraging surroundings who still succeeded, and who are now held up as models. No boy or girl, Marden insists, can learn too early the value of time and of opportunities within reach. Readers get an encouraging school reader, full of short examples of grit, work, and character, meant to be read in class or at home.
4627-the-lights-and-shadows-of-real-life:
T. S. Arthur published The Lights and Shadows of Real Life in 1851, opening with a preface on light and shadow in human life. To all who pass through the world come light and shadow, he says, and though the sun may shine, clouds often intervene and cast deep shadows about our footsteps. Those clouds, he insists, arise from below, not from pure heavens. They spring out of the earth beneath rather than falling from above.

If nothing evil lived in the mind, Arthur argues, there would be no cloud in the sky of our being, only eternal sunshine. But the sky does not always stay dark. As the heart fills with better purposes through trial and pain, clouds disperse and blessed sunlight returns. Readers get a moral sketchbook in two parts, meant as consolation, and as a plain account of how character makes its own weather.
4660-timothy-crump-s-ward-a-story-of-ame:
Horatio Alger published Timothy Crump's Ward in 1866, as a story of American life. It opens on the last day of the year, with 1836 about to end, on a cold day with no snow but ground frozen into stiff ridges. The sun shone all day with little heat or comfort, and the first chapter introduces the Crumps, a poor household facing a landlord's visit and a New Year's present.

Later chapters bring a lucky rescue, an envelope and its contents, eight years and Ida's progress, a strange visitor, a journey, and unexpected quarters. Suspense, bad coin, doubts and fears, a flower-girl, a trap, a prison escape, and the law stepping in follow, before Ida is found. Readers get a classic Alger tale of a ward, a mystery of birth, and honest effort rewarded, in plain, brisk prose.
4673-notes-by-the-way-in-a-sailor-s-life:
Captain Arthur E. Knights published Notes by the Way in a Sailor's Life after writing letters from Hong Kong in 1898. Murray Bain, editor of the China Mail, had asked why Knights did not send him an occasional letter. Friends later urged him to put the notes in pamphlet form for distribution among friends. Knights asks readers to treat leniently the literary efforts of one who is a sailor and not a cleric.

Contents include a quick passage, a record long passage, and a voyage of misfortune. They go on to the beginning of the German navy, an incident in Hong Kong harbour, a singular meeting, and a little railway experience. Later notes cover life-saving, a telescope presented by the British government, the ship Bombay, Chinese politeness, and a Brazilian slaver. Readers get a sailor's plain, anecdotal memoir, full of ports, ships, and sea life.
4716-a-day-in-old-athens-a-picture-of-at:
William Stearns Davis, professor of ancient history at Minnesota, wrote A Day in Old Athens. It shows what an intelligent visitor would see and hear in ancient Athens, if translated by legerdemain to the fourth century before Christ. He picks the year 360 before Christ, not for special virtue. Athens then stood architecturally almost perfect, with civic and social life at their best, and few outward signs of later decadence after Macedon triumphed.

Chapters cover the physical setting, first sights, and the Agora. They go on to the Athenian house, women, costume, slaves, children, schoolboys, and physicians. Davis warns that rare happenings are omitted, and probable matters are sometimes stated as facts to avoid long explanations. Readers get a vivid, readable tour of daily Athenian life, useful before reading Greek history or drama, and easy to follow chapter by chapter.
4767-the-mayor-s-wife:
Anna Katherine Green wrote The Mayor's Wife as a mystery, from A Spy's Duty and Questions. Through In the Gable Window and Lights and Sounds, it moves to The Strange Neighbours Next Door and At the Stair-Head. A Moving Shadow, The Paragraph, Scraps, and A Glimmer of the Truth follow, with Bess, Searchings, and A Discovery.

In the Library, The Two Weird Sisters, The Morning News, and The Cry from the Stairs lead to Explanation, The Cipher, and Mercy. The Wife's Tale, The Sins of the Fathers, and Restitution close the book. Chapter one opens with the narrator, not without self-control, yet unable to hide anxiety. Miss Davies enters with an air of importance, bearing an unusually fine position to offer, while the narrator needs a position badly. Her calculating gaze lets nothing escape as she scans every face. Readers get a Green mystery of spying and neighbours.
4958-justice-in-the-by-ways-a-tale-of-li:
Tom Swiggs's seventh introduction aboard a brig opens this tale of life's by-ways, and the chapters that follow parade a varied company: Madame Flamingo and her distinguished patrons, Mr. Snivel the Accommodation Man, George Mullholland, and Anna, whose history slowly comes to light.

Reflections on the cure of vice sit beside scenes of citizens commingling in port towns and parlors. The work is cataloged without an author. Readers get a sprawling mid-nineteenth-century novel of rogues, reformers, and respectable folk, where justice is sought off the main roads of society rather than in its courts.
4962-the-story-of-germ-life:
Bacteriology developed with marvellous rapidity in the fifteen years before this book, and its author sets out to explain germ life to general readers. Bacteria, scarcely heard of outside scientific circles at the start of the 1880s, had become household words, and everyone who reads was beginning to recognize their relation to everyday life.

The organisms called bacteria form a small class of microscopic plants, including yeasts, and the book follows their habits, growth, and effects. No author appears in the catalog record. Readers get a clear early introduction to microbes, written when germ theory was still news and its promise for health was just coming into view.
4992-diddie-dumps-and-tot-or-plantation-:
Louise-Clarke Pyrnelle's Diddie, Dumps, and Tot gathers stories of plantation child life, opening with the three children themselves and Christmas on the old plantation. Mammy's story, Old Billy, Diddie's book, Uncle Snake-Bit Bob's Sunday school, and Poor Ann follow, with plantation games, visiting, and the Fourth of July.

A tale of how the woodpecker's head and the robin's breast came to be red, and Uncle Daniel's sermon at a plantation meeting, mix folklore with daily life. Pyrnelle writes from memory of the old South, in dialect and domestic detail. Readers get a children's book of its era, affectionate in tone and now valuable as a window on how that world was remembered.
5119-the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-a:
Charles Klein's novel, adapted from his stage play, tells an American story of power and revenge. A great financier, John Burkett Ryder, ruins a judge who ruled against him. The judge's daughter, Shirley Green, sets out to undo the wrong, armed with little but courage and knowledge of Ryder's past.

The title borrows Aesop's fable: the small creature may one day free the great one, or bring him down. Klein mixes courtroom drama, business intrigue, and romance, and the book captures an era when Americans argued fiercely about trusts and bought judges. The book asks whether wealth could ever be made to answer for itself.
5642-harry-heathcote-of-gangoil-a-tale-o:
Anthony Trollope wrote Harry Heathcote of Gangoil as a tale of Australian bush life, opening a fortnight before Christmas 1871. Harry, twenty-four, returns home to dinner about eight in the evening at Gangoil station. Contents run from a night's ride and Medlicot's mill through Harry's appeal, Boscobel, and the Brownbies of Boolabong, to a bush fight and Harry's triumphant return.

Sergeant Forrest and a conclusion close the short novel. Trollope writes station life, squatters, and bush conflict with his usual clarity. Readers get a compact Australian adventure, about a young settler defending his home and name.
5703-the-lord-of-death-and-the-queen-of-:
Homer Eon Flint's Lord of Death and Queen of Life continues his science romance in three parts, opening with a discovery and a sky cube. The first scene gathers four men. One of them sings a cheerful baritone line about an owl and a pussycat in a pea-green boat. A geologist growls an accompaniment from his university quartet days. From that light opening, speculation about life, death, and strange powers takes hold.

Here follows a pulp adventure where scientific ideas drive the plot and larger questions about mortality sit behind the action. Flint writes plainly and moves quickly, so the book suits fans of early science fiction who enjoy bold premises and cliffhangers. It pairs with The Emancipatrix, sharing its author, its spirit of inquiry, and its taste for wonder.
5733-autobiography-truth-and-fiction-rel:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe tells his own life in Truth and Fiction Relating to My Life, here in a multi-translator English edition. Translators include Thomas Carlyle, Henry Longfellow, Walter Scott, Bayard Taylor, and John Oxenford, among others, and the work runs in parts that follow Goethe from childhood through his formation as a poet. The title itself warns readers that memory and shaping art mix.

Readers meet Goethe's family, Frankfurt, early loves, studies, and first literary ambitions, told with the hindsight of a great writer looking back. The book is both memoir and self-portrait, frank about growth and selective about fact. It suits readers of Goethe, German literature, and literary autobiography, offering a direct route into the making of a major mind.
5832-recalled-to-life:
Recalled to Life opens with Una Callingham's first recollection, a strange scene from when she was eighteen, in her father's house, the Grange, at Woodbury. Una notes oddly that babyhood, childhood, girlhood, and school days were all blotted out by that one scene, leaving her memory to begin where others' memories end. From that blank, a mystery of identity, family, and lost years unfolds.

The volume offers a Victorian sensation novel of memory and recovery, where a young woman must piece together a life she cannot recall. The story favors suspense and domestic secrets over action, with each revelation reshaping the past. It suits readers who enjoy mysteries of identity, and fans of late Victorian fiction where the mind itself becomes the puzzle.
6093-far-away-and-long-ago-a-history-of-:
Hudson recalls his early life far away and long ago. He opens with earliest memories: the house where he was born, a singular ombu tree, a tree without a name, the plain, and the ghost of a murdered slave. An old sheep-dog playmate, a first riding lesson, cattle at evening, and his mother fill the scene.

A new home follows, with a winter journey, a prisoner in the barn, a plantation, a paradise of rats, and a beggar on horseback. Mr. Trigg the schoolmaster, double-natured, impersonates an old woman and reads Dickens before degenerating. Hudson writes childhood on the pampas with wonder and loss.
6119-an-outback-marriage-a-story-of-aust:
Andrew Barton Paterson, author of The Man from Snowy River, sets An Outback Marriage in Australian club, station, and bush life. Chapters open in the club, at a dinner for five, in push society, and at the old station, before the coming of an heiress and a coach accident.

Mr. Blake's relations, visitors at the homestead, a lawyer in the bush, and a walk in moonlight lead to a broken engagement and rivals. Red Mick and his sheep dogs, wild cattle, a consultation at Kiley's, and a legal battle follow. Paterson writes station life with humor, horses, and hard bargaining.
6200-the-greek-view-of-life:
G. Lowes Dickinson offers The Greek View of Life as a general introduction to Greek literature and thought, primarily for readers who do not know Greek. Since most modern readers can reach Greek culture only through translations, he hopes his attempt, aided by quotations from original authors, will not seem labor thrown away.

Dickinson believes Greek culture remains, as in the past, the most valuable element of a liberal education. He avoids controversial matter as far as possible, asking classical scholars to judge the book by its object and fitness, not by omissions. The sixth edition of 1909 keeps that modest, guiding aim.
6565-chaucer-s-official-life:
James Root Hulbert pieces together Geoffrey Chaucer's work life from rolls, records, and printed calendars of his day. Close Rolls and Life Records supply much of the ground, and Hulbert notes where he used prints rather than hard-to-reach originals in the Public Record Office. He asks the reader's grace for slips in a work built on so many small notes.

What emerges is Chaucer the public man, not just the poet: a servant of king and city, with posts, pay, and duties that shaped his days. The study is close and careful, aimed at readers who want fact over fancy. Chaucer's Official Life thus fills in the working years behind the verse, one record at a time.
6662-little-citizens-the-humours-of-scho:
Myra Kelly tells school life through the eyes of immigrant children in New York, with pictures by W. D. Stevens. Her tales bear titles like A Little Matter of Real Estate, The Uses of Adversity, A Christmas Present for a Lady, and Love Among the Blackboards. A prince of Hester Street and a passport to paradise add a fairy-tale touch to classroom days.

Kelly writes with humor and heart, catching children's speech and their teachers' patience. The humor never mocks the children; it honors their pluck and wit. Little Citizens is a warm, funny book of school stories, still fresh in its love for young newcomers.
676-the-battle-of-life:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas tale of love and sacrifice in this book, from the 1867 Chapman and Hall Works. The story opens on a long summer day when a fierce battle was fought in stalwart England. Its grass was stained and its stream run red, before the tale turns to two sisters and the men who love them. Years pass, and the battle's traces linger in the field.

Dickens writes with rich, lyrical prose, full of moonlight, wind, and memory. The tale asks what love costs and what it saves. It endures as a lesser-known Christmas book, where a battle's shadow gives way to a quiet, hard-won peace.
6945-marguerite-verne-or-scenes-from-can:
Agatha Armour sets these scenes from Canadian life in St John, New Brunswick, opening on a starry, cold New Year's Eve. The city sits on its rocky throne above a broad bay, and the narrator claims love of New Brunswick as apology enough for praise. She muses on the human wish to worship the great and titled, then answers it with pride in two titles: British subject and New Brunswicker.

The novel that follows draws on the manners, talk, and social pride of a colonial port town. Marguerite Verne moves through its households and seasons, where rank, faith, and local loyalty shape choices. Armour writes with affection for her province, and the book reads as a portrait of Canadian life in its own confident voice.
6999-how-to-live-a-holy-life:
C E Orr opens How to Live a Holy Life with devotional reading, arguing a person may almost be known by the books he reads. Habitual readers of bad books may fairly be judged bad, while readers of religious books may reasonably be presumed religious, since books shape thoughts and thoughts shape the man. Reading devotional literature thus aids a devotional life.

Too few, Orr fears, grasp how much a taste for spiritual books matters to spiritual growth.
