Dickinson owns that his title begs a question. Yet he believes it has a clear meaning. The phases of Greek civilization are varied. Still, they group themselves about certain main ideas. Those ideas can be told apart from the ideas that ruled other nations. He has tried to bring those main ideas into relief. He avoids matter of dispute as far as he can. He asks scholars to judge it by its fitness for its end.
the-heir-of-redclyffe: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote The Heir of Redclyffe, with a heading in the record dated 1853. The contents list chapters numbered 1 through 19, with no titles given for any of them. Only the title page and contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. A second record in the library carries the same title and author, and that record opens with the first chapter itself.
the-house-of-life:
Dante Gabriel Rossetti gathered his sonnets under this title. Part I carries the heading Youth and Change. The first sonnet defines the form itself. A sonnet is a moment's monument. It is a memorial carved in ivory or ebony. It is also a coin. Its face reveals the soul. Its reverse shows the power the soul serves.

The next sonnet is Love Enthroned. Love sits above Truth, Hope, Fame, Youth, and Life. His throne stands in breathless bowers. The kindred powers cannot dream of that place. Bridal Birth follows in the sequence. Readers who continue get a long meditation on love, time, and death. Rossetti builds it one strict fourteen-line room at a time.
the-lights-and-shadows-of-real-life:
T. S. Arthur published his sketches of life and character at Philadelphia in 1851, and his preface frames the title in moral weather. Light and shadow come to everyone, he says, yet clouds in a life rise from below, from evil in the mind, not from a pure heaven.

Trials can clear that sky as better purposes grow through pain. A publisher introduction adds a short autobiography of Arthur as a self made man who rose through patient labor against adverse pressure. His temperance tales and domestic stories aimed to push readers toward reform at home.
the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-americ: Charles Klein wrote the play behind this novel, and Arthur Hornblow novelized it for Grosset and Dunlap in August 1906. Only the front pages and the start of a bare contents list are present here, showing a frontispiece of Shirley appealing to Mr. Ryder to go to Washington and save her father life. A Pope couplet warns that judges and senators have been bought for gold. The novel itself cannot be read in this record.
the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-an-ame: Charles Klein wrote the play behind this novel, and Arthur Hornblow novelized it as a story of an American life. Only the title page and a bare contents list of fifteen chapters are present here, with no story text at all. Its Pope epigraph reads slightly differently from the companion record of this title, giving Senates where the other gives Senators. The tale of a senator daughter facing down a railroad magnate is absent from this record.
the-lord-of-death-and-the-queen-of-life:
Homer Eon Flint's The Lord of Death and the Queen of Life opens Part I, The Discovery, inside a remarkable car. Four men ride in it: a doctor who sings a cheerful baritone, a geologist peeling potatoes, an architect named Jackson, and Smith, the engineer, who tends machinery with an oil-can. Their car draws an anti-gravitation current through tunnels, and Jackson demands to know how Smith pulls electricity from the ether without blasting them all to cinders.

Smith answers that the air around the earth is full of electricity. He looks unimportant, mild, and good-humored, yet his skull holds an unusually complete knowledge of electricity and mechanisms. Flint starts his science-fiction tale as a working trip among friends, with the wonder explained over song and potatoes.
the-mayor-s-wife:
Anna Katherine Green's novel The Mayor's Wife opens with a young woman badly in need of a position. She watches Miss Davies, who runs an employment office, enter with the air of someone carrying an unusually fine offer. The narrator admits she cannot hide all traces of her anxiety. Others in the room need work less desperately than she does.

The contents map the mystery she walks into: strange neighbors next door, a moving shadow, and scraps of evidence. Later chapters promise a cipher, a wife's tale, the sins of the fathers, and a finger on the wall. Titles such as In the Gable Window and The Cry from the Stairs keep the suspense domestic and close. Green, a pioneer of detective fiction, builds her puzzle inside a mayor's household, where a hired companion watches everything.
the-nervous-housewife:
Abraham Myerson's The Nervous Housewife was published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in November 1920. Its contents map a study in thirteen chapters. They cover the nature of nervousness and the types of housewife predisposed to it. Housework and the home appear as factors in the neurosis, and poverty's effects on the mind get a chapter. Later chapters treat the housewife and her husband, symptoms used as weapons against the husband, case histories, treatment, and the future of woman, the home, and marriage.

Chapter I opens by asking how long the problem of the nervous housewife has existed. Myerson wonders, half in jest, whether the cave man's wife wept over her house-cleaning or complained of her back when he returned from a prehistoric hunt. The problem, the opening implies, may be as old as the home itself.
the-oregon-trail-sketches-of-prairie-and: Francis Parkman, Jr. wrote The Oregon Trail, sketches of prairie and Rocky Mountain life. A contents list is what is present; the narrative itself is absent. The list runs to twenty-two chapters, from The Frontier and Fort Leavenworth to Tete Rouge, the volunteer. Titles trace the westward road: Jumping Off, The Platte and the Desert, The Buffalo, Scenes at Fort Laramie, war parties, trappers, the Black Hills, and the Pueblo and Bent's Fort.
the-path-of-life:
Stijn Streuvels wrote The Path of Life in West-Flemish, and Alexander Teixeira de Mattos translated it into English. In his translator's note, de Mattos calls Streuvels the most distinguished Low-Dutch author of the time, more read in Holland than in his own Belgium. He goes further, naming him the greatest living writer of imaginative prose in any land.

The note lingers on the West-Flemish dialect, spoken by about a million people between the North Sea, the French frontier, and a line near Bruges and Ghent. De Mattos praises its medieval words for fine shades of feeling, down to a word for the irritation felt when silk tears. The stories come from that sturdy, beautiful speech.
the-pilot-and-his-wife:
Jonas Lie's The Pilot and His Wife reached English readers in G. L. Tottenham's translation from the Norwegian. William Blackwood and Sons published it at Edinburgh and London in 1877. Tottenham's name is printed on this record's own title page. Chapter I opens off Arendal, on Norway's stern southern coast with its pine woods. Far out at sea stand the white walls of two lighthouses, the Great and the Little Torungen, each on its own bare rock island.

Spray drives against those walls in storms. Winter ice can cut the islands off from the land for long stretches. The chapter then looks back some twenty years before the Little Torungen light was built. A low house already stood on the island then. Its back was sunk into a heap of stones, and two small windows faced the sea. A boat lay drawn up in a cleft above the seaweed.
the-plain-man-and-his-wife:
Arnold Bennett's The Plain Man and His Wife, published at New York by George H. Doran Company, collects four essays. Their titles are All Means and No End, The Taste for Pleasure, The Risks of Life, and In Her Place. Bennett is named on the title page as the author of The Old Wives' Tale and Buried Alive.

The first essay opens with the plain man waking on a plain day and greeting it as another grind. Bennett insists the plain man means almost every man, rich or poor, successful or idle, luxurious or austere. Digestion has its limits, and no one can wear two neckties at once. Wealth brings its own insecurity and responsibility. Before breakfast even arrives, the tyrannic routine of the day has begun. The essays take ordinary married life from that unpromising start.
the-pleasures-of-life: Sir John Lubbock's The Pleasures of Life appears here through its contents alone. Only the chapter list is present, so the essays themselves do not appear. Part I opens with The Duty of Happiness and The Happiness of Duty. It then turns to a song of books, the choice of books, and the blessing of friends. Further chapters treat the value of time, the pleasures of travel and of home, science, and education. Part II begins with a chapter on ambition, and its remaining entries are not shown.
the-prairie-wife: Arthur Stringer's The Prairie Wife was issued by A. L. Burt Company at New York under 1915 copyrights, with a colour frontispiece by H. T. Dunn. The dedication, to Van, who knows and loves the West, faces a contents list built from dates rather than chapter titles. Entries run Thursday the Nineteenth, Saturday the Twenty-first, and on through the following weeks. That diary shape is all the opening shows. The entries themselves, and the prairie household they record, are not on view here.
the-promise-of-american-life: Herbert Croly's The Promise of American Life was published by Macmillan in November 1909 and reprinted three times by 1912. It is dedicated to the memory of David Goodman Croly. The contents open by asking what the promise of American life is, then turn to the Federalists and Republicans, and the Democrats and Whigs. Later chapters treat slavery and nationality, reform, and reconstruction. The pages at hand stop within that contents list; Croly's argument itself is not shown.
the-quest-of-the-simple-life:
W. J. Dawson argues for a simpler way of living. E. P. Dutton issued his volume at New York in 1907. Chapter headings call modern conditions a house of bondage. They ask how to get the best out of life. They ask how getting a living can join with living itself. They also ask how earth-hunger shapes people.

Further chapters join health to economics. They go in search of the picturesque. A line from Virgil stands as the motto. Readers tired of city pressure will recognize the appeal. Dawson's Edwardian phrasing shows the longing is old. People wanted a quieter life long before the present age.
the-relation-of-literature-to-life:
Charles Dudley Warner's essay is preceded by a biographical sketch from Thomas R. Lounsbury describing Franklin County in northwestern Massachusetts. Lounsbury paints small villages, poor roads, stony fields, and a Puritan stock given to plain living more than high thinking.

Dancing counted as immoral in those communities, cards led to gambling, and theatre-going drew suspicion, while Christmas itself was tolerated as a popish invention. That upbringing frames Warner's later question about what literature does for life. Readers get regional portraiture and cultural criticism joined together, with New England conscience as the starting point.
the-son-of-clemenceau-a-novel-of-modern-:
Alexander Dumas fils wrote this novel as a sequel to The Clemenceau Case, carrying the earlier story of modern love and life into a new generation. Its opening chapter, headed Student and Soldier, places a young wanderer in Munich at sunset. The evening gun has sounded from the fortifications, and cold March air moves over the plain of the Isar.

The young man lingers in the southern, unfashionable quarter, studying old burgher houses with blocked windows, stucco tablets, and faded frescoes. Few peasants and shopkeepers remain in the darkening streets, so his solitary walk sets the mood for a story rooted in the old city and its past.
the-story-of-germ-life:
H. W. Conn, professor of biology at Wesleyan University, wrote this little manual of bacteriology, and his preface of July 1915 reports how public understanding had changed since the first edition. Experimental medicine kept adding diseases caused by bacteria. Hygiene improved as the list grew. Colleges and high schools now teach the germ's importance widely. So do schools of farming and home science.

Conn stresses the friendly bacteria as well. He shows the huge part they play in industry and the arts. His chapters begin with the nature of bacteria. They set out the germ's place in the scale of life. They move through its work in the arts, the dairy, and farming. They end with disease. The methods of preventive medicine close the book.
the-web-of-life:
Robert Herrick, author of The Gospel of Freedom, opens The Web of Life in a Chicago hospital. A young surgeon examines a patient on a chair in the small receiving room of St. Isidore's, testing the flesh deftly with his fingers. The head nurse moves an incandescent light for him, weary and languid, while a younger nurse watches from the cot's foot, sweating with heat more than sympathy.

The delayed Chicago spring has blazed suddenly in late March, and no air stirs through the open lake-facing windows. Iodoform and ether thicken the room. The patient groans once, then sinks into the laboured breathing of drink or heavy pain. Herrick begins his novel inside medicine's close, exhausted machinery.
the-wheel-of-life: Ellen Glasgow, author of The Deliverance, The Battle-Ground, and The Ancient Law, published The Wheel of Life with Doubleday, Page in 1906. A dedication addresses her brother James Gibson Glasgow, mourning a brother loved and absent, dated New York, May 1905. The pages present here give the dedication and the start of a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. Part one, called The Romantic, begins with a chapter titled Pale Dawn, and part two is called The Sentimental. The section titles chart a love story's phases.
the-winning-of-canada-a-chronicle-of-wol:
William Wood wrote The Winning of Canada as a chronicle of Wolfe for the Chronicles of Canada series, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton. Published at Toronto in 1915, it is volume eleven of thirty-two. An author's note signed at Quebec in April 1914 explains Wood's method.

A life of Wolfe, Wood argues, is falsified if his military work is treated as complete in itself. Wolfe worked alongside the fleet in a war run on naval strategy throughout and tied to worldwide affairs. Only arrangement and expression are simplified in the sketch, drawn straight from original sources. Contents chapters run from the boy of 1727 through Louisbourg and Quebec to the Plains of Abraham.
the-world-as-i-have-found-it-sequel-to-i:
Mary L. Day Arms wrote The World As I Have Found It, published in Baltimore in 1878. The book continues her earlier Incidents in the Life of a Blind Girl. Rev. Charles F. Deems supplied an introduction. Deems notes that her first volume sold widely. Readers of it, he expects, will want news of her life since. Her patient perseverance under privations won her many friends.

Deems says the title page itself shows the book hardly needs introduction. Its author writes from blindness and hardship. Friends will gladly procure and preserve the sequel, he predicts. The memoir offers a nineteenth-century blind woman's own account. Such first-person disability narratives from the period remain uncommon and valuable.
the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-04-the-hi: Volume four of The World's Best Poetry, The Higher Life, appears here through its title pages and one heading. Bliss Carman edited the ten-volume 1904 set. Washington Gladden contributes an essay called Religion and Poetry. A notice of copyrights follows that heading. The poems of the volume do not appear in what appears here, so its selections cannot be described from them.
three-months-of-my-life: J. F. Foster, assistant-surgeon in Her Majesty's 36th Foot, kept the diary printed as Three Months of My Life. Lizzie A. Freeth edited it, and printers in Guernsey and London issued it in 1873. Foster expected to die and asked relatives to correct his hurried spelling. His dedication thanks God for preserving him through years of service in India and bringing him home. He gives the book to his parents, expecting affectionate reading. The editor's preface only begins in what is present, so Foster's diary entries themselves do not appear.
timothy-crump-s-ward-a-story-of-american:
Horatio Alger published Timothy Crump's Ward, a story of American life, in 1866. Contents promise twenty-seven chapters, from introducing the Crumps through a landlord's visit, a lucky rescue, eight years of Ida's progress, bad coin, traps, escapes, and a conclusion. Chapter one opens on the last day of the year.

Only hours remain before 1836 ends, on a cold day with frozen ground and no snow. The ward of the title, Ida, is found and lost again across the headings. Readers get an early Alger tale of a poor household, a mysterious child, and American city life.
two-knapsacks-a-novel-of-canadian-summer:
J. Cawdor Bell's Two Knapsacks, a novel of Canadian summer life, was entered at Toronto in 1892. A publishers' note introduces Bell as a new and promising native author. The note stakes the book's welcome on its character drawings across Canadian society.

Its dialect, the publishers boast, covers Irish, Scotch, English, Canadian, French, Southern, and Negro speech. Bell shows a remarkable acquaintance with English literature, especially Wordsworth. Torontonians and readers from the districts described get special interest, the note promises. Chapter one follows the note at once, and the summer tramp of the two knapsackers begins.
venetian-life:
William Dean Howells wrote Venetian Life from what he saw while living in Venice. A note to the second edition, signed at Cambridge on January 1, 1867, tells what he changed. He added a chapter on the history of Venetian commerce and the city's present trade. He enlarged the chapter on national holidays. He also gave the book an index of the chief people, events, and places it names.

Howells insists that the book's worth lies in its faithfulness to what he actually saw and knew. Great events of the past summer had changed Venice's fortunes, he grants. They had not, he thinks, changed the traits of her daily life he loved to watch. The contents run from arrival and first days through winter, opera, and dinners. Housekeeping and a balcony on the Grand Canal follow. Readers get a consul's close, fond record of a city in transition.
wallace-my-life:
Alfred Russel Wallace published My Life in 1905, with a revised edition in 1908, looking back on ninety years. Wallace had shared the discovery of natural selection with Darwin. He was also a land reformer, a socialist, and a believer in spiritualism.

He recalls his surveying years, his collecting in the Amazon, and the fire that sank his ship and specimens. The Malay Archipelago years and the famous letter to Darwin form the heart of the book. Later chapters argue his causes with undimmed zeal. The memoir shows a gentler, stranger, and more radical mind than Darwin's public image allows.
way-down-east-a-romance-of-new-england-l: Joseph R. Grismer wrote 'Way Down East, a romance of New England life. The book rests on Lottie Blair Parker's very successful play of the same title, with copyright in 1900. Grosset and Dunlap at New York issued it with scenes from D. W. Griffith's motion picture of the story. Lillian Gish as Anna Moore stands at the frontispiece. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of the contents only. Early chapters promise a conquering hero. A mock marriage and a glimpse of the garden of Eden follow.
within-an-inch-of-his-life:
Emile Gaboriau wrote this French detective novel, shown here in a 1913 Scribner edition. The first part, called Fire at Valpinson, opens on a June night in 1871. A bareheaded peasant rides bareback into Sauveterre at one in the morning. He pounds on the mayor's door and demands to see him at once.

Mayor Seneschal comes down in a dressing gown, candle in hand, already troubled. That alarm sets a crime inquiry in motion. Gaboriau builds the case through small town reactions and careful detail. Readers who like early detective fiction get a slow, tense start.
